item.title: Microsoft Foundry May 2026: The Updates I’d Actually Watch Closely
item.author: Emiliano Montesdeoca
item.description: The latest Microsoft Foundry roundup covers a lot, but the most important threads are trace-based evaluation, new model choice, managed isolation, and the continued rise of local and production-grade agent tooling.
item.content:encoded:
Monthly platform roundups can turn into feature overload pretty quickly.

So here is the shorter version of What’s New in Microsoft Foundry | May 2026: the platform is getting deeper in exactly the areas that matter most for real AI systems.

The threads I would watch are:

  • trace-based evaluation
  • broader model choice
  • stronger agent tooling
  • better managed isolation and cost visibility
  • continued momentum around local AI through Foundry Local

This is a dense roundup, so the pattern matters more than the count

There are a lot of individual bullets in the original article.

That is fine, but I do not think the best way to read this kind of post is feature-by-feature.

The better question is: what direction is the platform clearly reinforcing?

And I think the answer is this:

Foundry keeps getting stronger in the operational layers around agents, not just in the catalog of models.

That is a very good sign.

The most important theme is trace-based evaluation

If I had to pick one theme from the whole roundup, it would probably be trace-based evaluation.

Why? Because it changes the evaluation story from:

  • build a static dataset
  • run a benchmark
  • hope it reflects production

to something more realistic:

  • observe real behavior
  • evaluate real traces
  • learn from what the system is actually doing

That is a much more mature model for production AI.

Model breadth matters, but only if it stays operable

The additions around Grok, DeepSeek, Fireworks, and reinforcement fine-tuning are all useful in their own way.

But for me, the more important point is not that one more model has landed.

It is that model breadth is being combined with:

  • operational visibility
  • evaluation tooling
  • governance surfaces
  • deployment consistency

That is what keeps a model ecosystem from turning into chaos.

Foundry Local is becoming a recurring strategic signal

Another thing I would not ignore is how often Foundry Local now shows up as a serious part of the Foundry story.

That tells me Microsoft does not see local AI as a side experiment anymore.

It is becoming part of the broader platform narrative:

  • privacy
  • device-local inference
  • hardware portability
  • edge deployment
  • hybrid operational models

That is worth paying attention to.

My take

The details matter, but the bigger pattern matters more.

Foundry keeps moving toward a platform where agents, evaluations, models, local runtimes, and governance all connect more naturally.

That is the direction I care about most.

And this roundup, more than many of the smaller individual announcements, makes that direction easier to see in one place.

Original post: What’s new in Microsoft Foundry | May 2026

item.title: Foundry Local 1.1: Real-Time Transcription, Embeddings, and the Responses API
item.author: Emiliano Montesdeoca
item.description: Foundry Local 1.1 adds live microphone transcription, text embeddings, and Responses API support — all running locally with no cloud dependency, no network latency, no per-token cost.
item.content:encoded:
Foundry Local 1.0 proved the concept: run AI models locally on Windows, macOS (Apple Silicon), and Linux x64 with a developer-friendly SDK. Version 1.1 adds three capabilities that cover a lot of real production use cases.

Live Audio Transcription

The most significant new feature: real-time speech-to-text streaming directly from the microphone. Captions, voice UIs, meeting transcription, accessibility tooling — all running locally with zero cloud dependency.

The API is session-based and streams results as they arrive, with is_final markers to distinguish interim from finalized text. Available across all language bindings: JavaScript, C#, Python, and Rust.

Load a streaming speech model from the catalog, create a session with audio settings (sample rate, channels, language), start it, push raw PCM audio chunks, and consume the async stream of results. The post has full Python and C# examples.

Text Embeddings

Semantic search, RAG pipelines, clustering, similarity matching — these all require embeddings. Foundry Local 1.1 adds embedding model support so you can generate vectors locally from the same SDK, without sending data to a cloud endpoint.

For applications where data residency matters or where you’re processing sensitive content, local embedding generation is a meaningful capability.

Responses API

Foundry Local now supports the Responses API — the structured interface designed for agentic interactions. This adds:

  • Tool calling — let locally-running models invoke tools you define
  • Multimodal vision-language input — pass image + text to vision-capable models
  • Compatible with the standard API shape, so existing agents targeting OpenAI’s Responses API work against local models

Package Size Improvements

Two changes reduce the JavaScript package size:

  • The koffi FFI layer has been replaced with a custom Node-API C addon
  • WebGPU execution provider ships as a separate plugin, so applications that don’t need GPU acceleration don’t pay the size cost

The C# SDK now targets lower framework versions for broader .NET compatibility.

Why This Matters

The three capabilities together — transcription, embeddings, tool calling — cover the core building blocks of many AI applications. Running them locally means:

  • No internet required
  • No per-token costs
  • No data leaving the machine
  • Consistent latency regardless of network conditions

Foundry Local is the right choice for edge scenarios, privacy-sensitive workloads, offline applications, or anything where you want to avoid cloud dependency during development.

Original post: Foundry Local 1.1: Live Transcription, Embeddings, and Responses API
